key_concepts: Setting dy/dx=0 to find x-coordinates
Finding the corresponding y-coordinate
Types: maximum, minimum, point of inflection

definitions.definition: A point on a curve where the gradient (dy/dx) equals zero.

formulas: Solve dy/dx = 0 for x, then substitute to find y

explanation: A maximum point is a stationary point where the curve changes from increasing to decreasing, representing a local peak, identifiable via sign changes in the gradient or a negative second derivative.
key_concepts: Gradient changes from positive to negative
Second derivative test: f''(x)<0
Local vs global maximum

definitions.definition: A stationary point where the function value is greater than at nearby points, with the gradient changing from positive to negative.

formulas: At a maximum: dy/dx=0 and d²y/dx²<0

worked_examples.problem: Show that (2,5) is a maximum for y=-x²+4x+1
worked_examples.answer: Since the second derivative is negative, (2,5) is a maximum

worked_examples.problem: Find and classify the stationary point of y=-x³+3x²
worked_examples.answer: (2,4) is a maximum, since d²y/dx²=-6<0 there

practice_questions.q: Verify (0,0) is a maximum for y=-x²
practice_questions.answer: dy/dx=-2x=0 at x=0; d²y/dx²=-2<0, confirmed maximum

practice_questions.q: Find the maximum point of y=-x²+6x
Find the maximum point of y=-2x²+8x-3

Find the maximum point of y=9-x²

exam_style_questions.q: Find the coordinates of the maximum point of y=-x³+3x²+9x-2, using the second derivative test to confirm.
exam_style_questions.answer: dy/dx=-3x²+6x+9=0; x²-2x-3=0; (x-3)(x+1)=0; x=3 or x=-1; d²y/dx²=-6x+6; at x=3: -12<0 (maximum); at x=-1: 12>0 (minimum); maximum point: y(3)=-27+27+27-2=25; maximum at (3,25)

exam_style_questions.q: A company's profit is modelled by P(x)=-2x²+40x-150, where x is the number of units sold (hundreds). Find the maximum profit and the corresponding value of x, using calculus.
exam_style_questions.answer: dP/dx=-4x+40=0; x=10; d²P/dx²=-4<0, confirming maximum; P(10)=-200+400-150=50; maximum profit is 50 (thousand) at x=10 (1000 units)

common_mistakes: Assuming any stationary point is automatically a maximum without checking the second derivative or sign change
Sign errors when computing or interpreting the second derivative
Confusing a local maximum (peak relative to nearby points) with the overall highest value of the function (global maximum), which may not exist or may be different
tips: Always verify a stationary point is genuinely a maximum using the second derivative test (or a sign-change table) — don't assume
d²y/dx²<0 at a stationary point confirms a maximum; d²y/dx²>0 confirms a minimum
For functions without a clear domain restriction, a 'maximum' found this way is typically only a LOCAL maximum, not necessarily the highest value overall
summary: Maximum points represent local peaks in a curve's behaviour, rigorously confirmed via the second derivative test — a cornerstone technique for optimisation problems.
quick_revision: Maximum: dy/dx=0 and d²y/dx²<0
Gradient changes from positive to negative
Local maximum ≠ necessarily the global maximum

explanation: A minimum point is a stationary point where the curve changes from decreasing to increasing, representing a local trough, identifiable via sign changes in the gradient or a positive second derivative.
key_concepts: Gradient changes from negative to positive
Second derivative test: f''(x)>0
Local vs global minimum

definitions.definition: A stationary point where the function value is less than at nearby points, with the gradient changing from negative to positive.

formulas: At a minimum: dy/dx=0 and d²y/dx²>0

worked_examples.problem: Show that (2,-1) is a minimum for y=x²-4x+3
worked_examples.answer: Since the second derivative is positive, (2,-1) is a minimum

worked_examples.problem: Find and classify the stationary point of y=x³-3x²+5
worked_examples.answer: (2,1) is a minimum, since d²y/dx²=6>0 there

practice_questions.q: Verify (0,0) is a minimum for y=x²
practice_questions.answer: dy/dx=2x=0 at x=0; d²y/dx²=2>0, confirmed minimum

practice_questions.q: Find the minimum point of y=x²-8x

exam_style_questions.q: Find the coordinates of the minimum point of y=x³-6x²+9x+1, using the second derivative test to confirm your classification.
exam_style_questions.answer: dy/dx=3x²-12x+9=0; x²-4x+3=0; (x-1)(x-3)=0; x=1 or x=3; d²y/dx²=6x-12; at x=1: -6<0 (maximum); at x=3: 6>0 (minimum); minimum: y(3)=27-54+27+1=1; minimum at (3,1)

exam_style_questions.q: The cost of manufacturing x units is modelled by C(x)=x²-40x+500. Find the number of units minimising cost, and the minimum cost, using calculus.
exam_style_questions.answer: dC/dx=2x-40=0; x=20; d²C/dx²=2>0, confirming minimum; C(20)=400-800+500=100; minimum cost is 100 at x=20 units

common_mistakes: Assuming a stationary point is a minimum without verification via the second derivative or sign change
Sign errors leading to incorrect classification (mixing up positive and negative conclusions)
Confusing local minimum with the function's overall lowest value (global minimum), which may differ
tips: Always confirm minimum classification using d²y/dx²>0, rather than assuming from context alone
This technique is the standard approach for cost-minimisation and similar optimisation problems in applied contexts
Remember: a local minimum only guarantees the lowest value NEARBY, not necessarily across the function's entire domain
summary: Minimum points, rigorously identified via the second derivative test, are essential for solving real-world cost-minimisation and general optimisation problems using calculus.
quick_revision: Minimum: dy/dx=0 and d²y/dx²>0
Gradient changes from negative to positive
Local minimum ≠ necessarily the global minimum

explanation: Classifying stationary points determines whether each is a maximum, minimum, or point of inflection, using either the second derivative test or a sign-change (nature) table of the first derivative.
key_concepts: Second derivative test (fast, but inconclusive if zero)
Sign-change table method (always conclusive)
Points of inflection (where the classification tests give ambiguous or zero results)

definitions.definition: A method for classifying stationary points: f''(x)>0 indicates a minimum, f''(x)<0 indicates a maximum, and f''(x)=0 is inconclusive (requires further investigation).

formulas: f''(x)>0: minimum; f''(x)<0: maximum; f''(x)=0: use sign-change table

worked_examples.problem: Classify the stationary points of y=x⁴ at x=0 using the second derivative test
steps: Use sign-change table: y' is negative for x<0, positive for x>0
worked_examples.answer: Minimum (confirmed by sign change, despite the inconclusive second derivative test)

worked_examples.problem: Classify the stationary point of y=x³ at x=0
steps: Sign-change table: y' is positive on both sides of x=0
worked_examples.answer: Point of inflection (not a maximum or minimum, since the gradient doesn't change sign)

practice_questions.q: Classify the stationary point of y=x²+1 at x=0 using d²y/dx²
Classify the stationary point of y=-x²+3 at x=0
Explain when the second derivative test is inconclusive
practice_questions.answer: When d²y/dx²=0 at the stationary point

practice_questions.q: State the alternative method to use when the second derivative test is inconclusive
practice_questions.answer: The sign-change (nature) table of the first derivative

practice_questions.q: Classify a stationary point where the gradient is negative before and positive after

exam_style_questions.q: Find and classify all stationary points of y=3x⁴-4x³, explaining any case where the second derivative test is inconclusive.
exam_style_questions.answer: dy/dx=12x³-12x²=12x²(x-1)=0; x=0 or x=1; d²y/dx²=36x²-24x; at x=1: 36-24=12>0 (minimum); at x=0: 0 (inconclusive) — use sign-change table: for x slightly less than 0, dy/dx=12x²(x-1) is negative (since x²>0, x-1<0); for x slightly more than 0 (but less than 1), dy/dx is still negative (x-1<0 still); since the sign doesn't change across x=0, this is a point of inflection, not a max or min

exam_style_questions.q: A curve has stationary points at x=-2 and x=3. Given d²y/dx²=6x-6, classify each stationary point.
exam_style_questions.answer: At x=-2: d²y/dx²=6(-2)-6=-18<0, maximum; at x=3: d²y/dx²=6(3)-6=12>0, minimum

common_mistakes: Relying solely on the second derivative test even when it gives zero (inconclusive), without falling back to the sign-change table
Errors constructing or interpreting the sign-change table (checking gradient sign at points just before and after the stationary point)
Confusing a point of inflection with a genuine maximum or minimum
tips: Always attempt the second derivative test first — it's faster when conclusive
If d²y/dx²=0, you MUST use a sign-change (nature) table of dy/dx to properly classify the point — don't skip this
A point of inflection occurs when the gradient does NOT change sign across the stationary point (stays positive or stays negative on both sides)
summary: Systematic classification combines the fast second derivative test with the always-reliable sign-change table, ensuring every stationary point is correctly identified even in ambiguous cases.
quick_revision: Second derivative test: f''>0 min, f''<0 max, f''=0 inconclusive
If inconclusive, use a sign-change table of dy/dx
No sign change = point of inflection, not max/min

explanation: A function is increasing over an interval if its derivative is positive throughout that interval, meaning the function's output rises as x increases.
key_concepts: dy/dx > 0 defines an increasing interval
Strictly increasing vs non-decreasing
Finding intervals of increase by analysing the derivative's sign

definitions.definition: A function f is increasing on an interval if f'(x) > 0 for all x in that interval.

formulas: f is increasing where f'(x) > 0

worked_examples.problem: Find the interval where y=x²-4x is increasing
Show that y=x³ is increasing for all x
steps: dy/dx=3x², which is ≥0 for all x, and >0 except at x=0
worked_examples.answer: y is increasing for all x (since 3x²≥0, with equality only at the single point x=0)

practice_questions.q: Find where y=x²-6x is increasing

Show that f(x)=x³+3x+1 is increasing for all real x, without finding any stationary points.
exam_style_questions.answer: f'(x)=3x²+3=3(x²+1); since x²≥0 for all x, x²+1≥1>0 always, so f'(x)>0 for all x, confirming f is increasing everywhere (and has no stationary points, since f'(x) is never zero)

common_mistakes: Solving the inequality dy/dx>0 incorrectly, especially for quadratic or higher-degree derivatives

Forgetting to state the answer as an interval or range of x, not just a single critical value
tips: Solve f'(x)>0 as an inequality — the same techniques from quadratic/polynomial inequalities apply directly here
'Increasing' refers to the function's behaviour (rising as x increases), completely independent of whether the function's VALUES are positive or negative
Always express your final answer as a range of x-values (an interval), not a single number

explanation: Curve sketching combines multiple calculus and algebraic techniques — intercepts, stationary points, asymptotes, and end behaviour — to produce an accurate graph of a function without needing to plot numerous individual points.
key_concepts: Finding intercepts (x and y)
Finding and classifying stationary points
Considering end behaviour and any asymptotes

definitions.definition: The process of producing an accurate graph of a function using key algebraic and calculus-derived features rather than extensive point-by-point plotting.

formulas: Combines: intercepts, dy/dx=0 (stationary points), d²y/dx² (classification), limiting behaviour

worked_examples.problem: Sketch the key features of y=x³-3x²
worked_examples.answer: Key features: touches x-axis at (0,0) [double root, also a max], crosses at (3,0); local max (0,0), local min (2,-4)

worked_examples.problem: Describe the end behaviour of y=x³-3x²

exam_style_questions.q: Sketch the curve y=x³-3x+2, finding and labelling all intercepts and stationary points, and stating the end behaviour.
exam_style_questions.answer: y-intercept (0,2); x-intercepts: factor as (x-1)²(x+2)=0, so x=1 (double) and x=-2; dy/dx=3x²-3=0, x=±1; d²y/dx²=6x; at x=1: 6>0 (min), y(1)=1-3+2=0, matching the double root; at x=-1: -6<0 (max), y(-1)=-1+3+2=4; end behaviour: as x→-∞,y→-∞; as x→∞,y→∞

exam_style_questions.q: Sketch the curve y=x²/(x-1), identifying any vertical or horizontal asymptotes, intercepts, and stationary points.
exam_style_questions.answer: Vertical asymptote at x=1 (denominator zero); as x→∞ or x→-∞, y behaves like x (since degree of numerator exceeds denominator by 1), suggesting an oblique asymptote y≈x+1 (found via division); x-intercept and y-intercept both at origin (0,0); stationary points found by setting dy/dx=0 using the quotient rule, giving further key points to plot

common_mistakes: Missing one or more key features (intercepts, stationary points, or asymptotes), leading to an inaccurate sketch
Errors in any of the individual sub-calculations (finding intercepts, solving dy/dx=0, classifying via d²y/dx²) propagating into the final sketch
Not considering end behaviour, resulting in a sketch that doesn't correctly show how the curve behaves far from the origin
tips: Work through features systematically: y-intercept, x-intercept(s), stationary points (found and classified), then end behaviour
Double-check each individual calculation before incorporating it into the final sketch — errors compound quickly in multi-step curve sketching
Always consider the degree and leading coefficient for end behaviour, and check for any vertical/horizontal asymptotes with rational functions
summary: Curve sketching is the practical culmination of algebra and calculus skills — systematically finding intercepts, stationary points, and end behaviour produces an accurate graph without extensive plotting.
quick_revision: Find y-intercept, x-intercept(s)
Find and classify stationary points (dy/dx=0, then d²y/dx²)
Determine end behaviour (and asymptotes for rational functions)

explanation: Concavity describes the curvature of a graph — concave up (like a smile, curving upward) where the second derivative is positive, and concave down (like a frown) where it is negative.
key_concepts: Concave up: f''(x)>0
Concave down: f''(x)<0
Relationship to the shape near maximum/minimum points

definitions.definition: The direction a curve bends: concave up (f''(x)>0) curves like a cup; concave down (f''(x)<0) curves like a cap.

formulas: Concave up: f''(x) > 0; Concave down: f''(x) < 0

worked_examples.problem: Determine the concavity of y=x² for all x
Determine the concavity of y=-x²+3x at x=1
worked_examples.answer: Concave down at x=1 (and everywhere, since y'' is constant)

exam_style_questions.q: Determine the intervals of concavity for y=x³-6x²+9x, by finding where the second derivative is positive and negative.
exam_style_questions.answer: y'=3x²-12x+9; y''=6x-12; y''>0 (concave up) when x>2; y''<0 (concave down) when x<2

exam_style_questions.q: Explain why a maximum point is always associated with concave down behaviour, and a minimum with concave up, using the second derivative test logic.
exam_style_questions.answer: At a maximum, the gradient changes from positive to negative, meaning the gradient itself is decreasing — this is exactly what a negative second derivative (concave down) represents; similarly, at a minimum the gradient increases from negative to positive, corresponding to a positive second derivative (concave up)

common_mistakes: Confusing concave up/down with increasing/decreasing (these describe different aspects of a curve's behaviour)
Sign errors when computing or interpreting the second derivative for concavity
Assuming concavity is constant throughout a curve's domain when it may actually change (as at a point of inflection)
tips: Concavity (curvature direction) is a distinct concept from monotonicity (increasing/decreasing) — a function can be increasing while concave up OR concave down
f''(x)>0 always means concave up (like a bowl/cup, holding water); f''(x)<0 means concave down (like a dome/cap)
Concavity can change across a function's domain — the point where this happens is a point of inflection
summary: Concavity, governed by the sign of the second derivative, describes a curve's bending direction — a concept distinct from but related to increasing/decreasing behaviour and stationary point classification.

explanation: A point of inflection is where a curve changes concavity (from concave up to concave down, or vice versa), typically found where the second derivative equals zero and changes sign.
key_concepts: Second derivative equals zero and changes sign
Not necessarily a stationary point (gradient may be non-zero)
Distinguishing from stationary points of inflection (where gradient is also zero)

definitions.definition: A point where a curve's concavity changes, typically identified where f''(x)=0 and the sign of f''(x) changes on either side.

formulas: Point of inflection: f''(x)=0, with a sign change in f''(x) either side

worked_examples.problem: Find the point of inflection of y=x³
steps: Check sign change: y''<0 for x<0, y''>0 for x>0

worked_examples.problem: Find the point of inflection of y=x³-6x²+9x
worked_examples.answer: x = 2 (find y-coordinate by substituting into the original equation for the full point)

practice_questions.q: Find where y''=0 for y=2x³-12x²

practice_questions.answer: f'' must actually change sign on either side of that point

practice_questions.q: Explain why x^4 does not have a point of inflection at x=0 despite y''(0)=0
practice_questions.answer: y''=12x² does not change sign at x=0 (it's non-negative on both sides), so concavity doesn't actually change there — not a genuine point of inflection

exam_style_questions.q: Find the point of inflection of y=x³-3x²+2, verifying using a sign-change check on the second derivative.
exam_style_questions.answer: y''=6x-6=0, x=1; check sign: for x<1, y''<0 (concave down); for x>1, y''>0 (concave up); sign change confirmed; y(1)=1-3+2=0; point of inflection at (1,0)

exam_style_questions.q: Explain why y=x⁴ does NOT have a point of inflection at x=0, despite y''(0)=0.
exam_style_questions.answer: y''=12x², which is always ≥0 and doesn't change sign at x=0 (it's zero there but positive on both sides); since concavity doesn't actually change, x=0 is not a genuine point of inflection, just a point where the second derivative test is inconclusive for a minimum

common_mistakes: Concluding a point of inflection exists simply because f''(x)=0, without verifying an actual sign change
Confusing points of inflection with all stationary points (they are related but distinct concepts)
Forgetting to find the y-coordinate to give the full point of inflection, not just the x-value
tips: f''(x)=0 alone is NOT sufficient — always verify the sign of f'' actually changes on either side to confirm a genuine point of inflection
A point of inflection can occur even where the gradient (dy/dx) is non-zero — it's fundamentally about concavity change, not gradient
Always state the full coordinate point, not just the x-value where the inflection occurs
summary: Points of inflection mark genuine changes in a curve's concavity, requiring careful sign-change verification beyond simply solving f''(x)=0.

Can occur where gradient is zero OR non-zero

explanation: A tangent to a curve at a given point touches the curve at that single point with a gradient equal to the curve's derivative there, found using differentiation combined with the point-slope line equation.
key_concepts: Gradient of tangent = dy/dx at that point
Combining differentiation with point-slope form
Tangent as a local linear approximation of the curve

definitions.definition: A straight line touching a curve at a single point, with gradient equal to the curve's derivative at that point.

formulas: y - y₁ = f'(x₁)(x - x₁), where (x₁,y₁) is the point of tangency

Find the tangent to y=x³-2x at x=1

exam_style_questions.q: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve y=x³-4x+1 at the point where x=2, and find where this tangent crosses the y-axis.
exam_style_questions.answer: y'=3x²-4; at x=2: 12-4=8; point: y(2)=8-8+1=1, so (2,1); tangent: y-1=8(x-2), y=8x-15; y-axis crossing: y=-15 (at x=0)

exam_style_questions.q: Find the equation of the tangent to y=ln(x) at x=e, and use it to approximate ln(e+0.1).
exam_style_questions.answer: y'=1/x; at x=e: gradient=1/e; point: (e,1); tangent: y-1=(1/e)(x-e), y=x/e; approximate ln(e+0.1) using tangent: y≈(e+0.1)/e=1+0.1/e≈1.0368

common_mistakes: Forgetting to find the actual point (x,y) on the curve before applying point-slope form
Confusing the tangent's gradient (from the derivative) with the gradient of a general secant/chord line
Sign or arithmetic errors when substituting into point-slope form
tips: Always find BOTH the derivative (for gradient) AND the actual point on the curve before writing the tangent equation
The tangent line provides a good LOCAL approximation of the curve near the point of tangency — useful for estimation problems
Simplify the final tangent equation to a clean, standard form (y=mx+c)
summary: Tangent lines combine differentiation (for gradient) with point-slope form (for the equation), a fundamental technique appearing throughout calculus applications.
quick_revision: Find gradient via f'(x₁)
Find the point (x₁,y₁) on the curve
Use point-slope form: y-y₁=f'(x₁)(x-x₁)

explanation: A normal to a curve at a given point is the line perpendicular to the tangent at that point, using the negative reciprocal of the tangent's gradient combined with point-slope form.
key_concepts: Normal gradient = -1/(tangent gradient)
Combining differentiation with the perpendicular gradient condition
Applications to finding intersection points and geometric properties

definitions.definition: The line perpendicular to the tangent of a curve at a given point.

formulas: Normal gradient = -1 / f'(x₁)
y - y₁ = [-1/f'(x₁)](x - x₁)

worked_examples.problem: Find the normal to y=x² at x=2
Find the normal to y=x³ at x=1

practice_questions.q: Find the normal to y=x² at x=1
Find the normal to y=x²-4 at x=0
practice_questions.answer: tangent gradient=0, normal is vertical: x=0

practice_questions.q: Find the normal to y=2x²+1 at x=1
practice_questions.answer: tangent gradient=4, normal gradient=-1/4; point (1,3); y-3=-1/4(x-1)

practice_questions.q: Find the normal to y=x³ at x=0
practice_questions.answer: tangent gradient=0, normal is vertical: x=0

practice_questions.q: Find the normal to y=√x at x=1
practice_questions.answer: tangent gradient=1/2, normal gradient=-2; point(1,1); y-1=-2(x-1)

exam_style_questions.q: Find the equation of the normal to the curve y=x³-3x+2 at the point where x=1, and find where this normal crosses the x-axis.
exam_style_questions.answer: y'=3x²-3; at x=1: 3-3=0; tangent is horizontal, so normal is VERTICAL: x=1 (this is already the x-axis crossing point itself, since a vertical line x=1 'crosses' the x-axis at (1,0) directly)

exam_style_questions.q: Find the equation of the normal to y=eˣ at x=0, and find its y-intercept.
exam_style_questions.answer: y'=eˣ; at x=0: gradient=1; normal gradient=-1; point (0,1); normal: y-1=-1(x-0), y=-x+1; y-intercept is (0,1) itself

common_mistakes: Using the tangent's gradient directly instead of taking its negative reciprocal
Forgetting the special case when the tangent gradient is 0 (giving a vertical normal) or undefined (giving a horizontal normal)
Sign errors in the point-slope form setup
tips: Always take the NEGATIVE RECIPROCAL of the tangent gradient (found via differentiation) to get the normal gradient
If the tangent gradient is 0 (horizontal tangent), the normal is a VERTICAL line (x=constant) — handle this special case directly
Find both the gradient and the point on the curve before constructing the normal equation, exactly as with tangents
summary: Normal lines apply the perpendicular gradient relationship to calculus-derived tangent gradients, a frequently tested combination of differentiation and coordinate geometry skills.
quick_revision: Normal gradient = -1/(tangent gradient)
Special case: horizontal tangent → vertical normal
Combine with point-slope form using the point on the curve

explanation: Finding the equation of a tangent is the complete, systematic process of combining differentiation (for gradient) with a given or found point on the curve, using point-slope form to write the final line equation.
key_concepts: Full systematic method: differentiate, evaluate, apply point-slope
Tangents at a given point vs. tangents passing through an external point
Simplifying the final equation to standard form

definitions.definition: The complete process of finding a tangent line: differentiate the curve, evaluate the gradient at the point of tangency, then apply point-slope form.

formulas: y - y₁ = f'(x₁)(x - x₁)

worked_examples.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to y=x²-3x+2 at x=4
Find the tangent to y=x³ passing through the origin (external point tangency, requiring the point of tangency to be found)
steps: Let point of tangency be (a,a³); gradient=3a²
a³=3a³, so a=0 (trivial) — no non-trivial external tangent exists through the origin in this specific case, since it lies ON the curve
worked_examples.answer: The only tangent through the origin is at (0,0) itself, since the origin lies on the curve y=x³

practice_questions.q: Find the tangent to y=x²+1 at x=2
Find the tangent to y=x³-x at x=1
Find the tangent to y=5-x² at x=1
Find the tangent to y=2x²-5x at x=0
Find the tangent to y=x²+2x-1 at x=-1

exam_style_questions.q: Find the equation of the tangent to y=x²-2x+3 at the point where x=3, and find the coordinates where this tangent intersects the curve y=x again (if anywhere other than the point of tangency).
exam_style_questions.answer: y'=2x-2; at x=3: 4; point(3,6); tangent: y-6=4(x-3), y=4x-6; find intersection with y=x²-2x+3: 4x-6=x²-2x+3; x²-6x+9=0; (x-3)²=0, x=3 (repeated root — confirms the tangent only touches at x=3, as expected for a genuine tangent)

exam_style_questions.q: The tangent to y=x²+k at x=2 passes through the point (0,-3). Find the value of k.
exam_style_questions.answer: y'=2x; at x=2, gradient=4; point on curve: (2,4+k); tangent: y-(4+k)=4(x-2); at x=0: y=(4+k)-8=-3; -4+k=-3; k=1

common_mistakes: Errors in any of the individual sub-steps (differentiation, evaluation, point-slope application) compounding into an incorrect final equation
Confusing tangent problems at a specific point (straightforward) with tangent problems through an external point (requiring solving for the unknown point of tangency)
Not simplifying the final equation into a clean, standard form
tips: Follow the systematic three-step method every time: differentiate, evaluate at the point, apply point-slope form
For 'tangent through an external point' problems, set up the point of tangency as an unknown (a, f(a)) and solve using the tangent condition
Always simplify your final tangent equation into y=mx+c or a similarly clean standard form
summary: This topic represents the complete, systematic application of differentiation to find tangent equations — a core, frequently examined skill throughout Add Maths calculus.
quick_revision: 1. Differentiate the curve
2. Evaluate the derivative at the point of tangency
3. Apply point-slope form, then simplify

explanation: Finding the equation of a normal is the complete, systematic process combining differentiation, the perpendicular gradient relationship, and point-slope form to write the final normal line equation.
key_concepts: Full systematic method: differentiate, find perpendicular gradient, apply point-slope
Applications to finding where normals intersect the curve or axes
Special cases with horizontal/vertical tangents

definitions.definition: The complete process of finding a normal line: differentiate the curve, find the perpendicular gradient at the point, then apply point-slope form.

formulas: y - y₁ = [-1/f'(x₁)](x - x₁)

worked_examples.problem: Find the normal to y=x²-3x+2 at x=4
Find where the normal to y=x² at x=1 crosses the x-axis
steps: y'=2x; at x=1, tangent gradient=2, normal gradient=-1/2

practice_questions.q: Find the normal to y=x²-1 at x=2
practice_questions.answer: tangent gradient=4, normal gradient=-1/4; point(2,3); y-3=-1/4(x-2)

practice_questions.q: Find the normal to y=x³-2x at x=1
practice_questions.answer: tangent gradient=1, normal gradient=-1; point(1,-1); y+1=-(x-1)

practice_questions.q: Find where the normal to y=x² at x=0 crosses the y-axis
practice_questions.answer: tangent gradient=0, normal is vertical x=0, which IS the y-axis

practice_questions.q: Find the normal to y=4-x² at x=1
practice_questions.answer: tangent gradient=-2, normal gradient=1/2; point(1,3); y-3=1/2(x-1)

practice_questions.q: Find the normal to y=2x² at x=-1
practice_questions.answer: tangent gradient=-4, normal gradient=1/4; point(-1,2); y-2=1/4(x+1)

exam_style_questions.q: Find the equation of the normal to y=x³-6x+5 at the point where x=2, and find where this normal crosses the y-axis.
exam_style_questions.answer: y'=3x²-6; at x=2: 12-6=6; normal gradient=-1/6; point: y(2)=8-12+5=1, so (2,1); normal: y-1=-1/6(x-2); y-axis crossing (x=0): y=1+1/3=4/3

exam_style_questions.q: The normal to y=x²+px+q at x=1 has gradient -1/4 and passes through (1,3). Find p and q.
exam_style_questions.answer: Normal gradient -1/4 means tangent gradient=4; y'=2x+p; at x=1: 2+p=4, p=2; y(1)=1+p+q=3; 1+2+q=3, q=0

common_mistakes: Forgetting to take the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient (a very common and critical error)
Errors in any sub-step (differentiation, gradient calculation, point-slope application) compounding into an incorrect final result
Not handling the special vertical/horizontal normal cases correctly when the tangent gradient is 0 or undefined
tips: Follow the systematic method every time: differentiate, find tangent gradient, take negative reciprocal for normal gradient, apply point-slope form
Always double-check by confirming your normal gradient is indeed the negative reciprocal, not the original tangent gradient
Handle horizontal tangent (→ vertical normal) and vertical tangent (→ horizontal normal) as explicit special cases
summary: This topic represents the complete, systematic application of differentiation and perpendicularity to find normal equations, frequently combined with further coordinate geometry in exam questions.
quick_revision: 1. Differentiate to find tangent gradient
2. Take negative reciprocal for normal gradient
3. Apply point-slope form, then simplify

topic: Rates of Change and Related Rates
explanation: Rates of change use differentiation to model how one quantity changes with respect to another (often time), while related rates connect multiple changing quantities through a shared equation, using the chain rule to relate their rates.
key_concepts: dy/dx (or dy/dt) as a rate of change
Setting up an equation connecting related quantities
Using the chain rule to relate different rates

definitions.definition: A technique connecting the rates of change of two or more related quantities, using differentiation and the chain rule.

formulas: Chain rule for related rates: dA/dt = (dA/dr)(dr/dt)

worked_examples.problem: A circle's radius increases at 2cm/s. Find the rate of increase of area when r=5cm.
A cube's side length increases at 3cm/s. Find the rate of increase of volume when the side is 4cm.

practice_questions.q: A square's side increases at 1cm/s. Find dA/dt when side=5cm (A=s²)
A sphere's radius increases at 0.5cm/s. Find dV/dt when r=3cm (V=(4/3)πr³)
State the chain rule formula for related rates connecting A and t via r
A circle's area increases at 10cm²/s. Find dr/dt when r=2cm
A cylinder's height increases at 2cm/s with fixed radius 3cm. Find dV/dt (V=πr²h)

exam_style_questions.q: Air is pumped into a spherical balloon at a rate of 100 cm³/s. Find the rate at which the radius is increasing when the radius is 5cm, given V=(4/3)πr³.
exam_style_questions.answer: dV/dr=4πr²; dV/dt=dV/dr×dr/dt; 100=4π(25)(dr/dt); dr/dt=100/(100π)=1/π cm/s

exam_style_questions.q: A ladder 5m long leans against a wall. The bottom of the ladder slides away from the wall at 0.5 m/s. Find the rate at which the top of the ladder is sliding down when the bottom is 3m from the wall, using x²+y²=25 (Pythagoras).
exam_style_questions.answer: Differentiate implicitly: 2x(dx/dt)+2y(dy/dt)=0; at x=3, y=4 (from Pythagoras); dx/dt=0.5; 2(3)(0.5)+2(4)(dy/dt)=0; 3+8(dy/dt)=0; dy/dt=-3/8 m/s (negative indicates the top is sliding down)

common_mistakes: Forgetting to apply the chain rule correctly when connecting the two related rates
Errors setting up the initial equation connecting the two quantities (e.g. using the wrong volume/area formula)
Sign errors, especially in problems involving decreasing quantities (rates should be negative)
tips: Always set up a clear equation connecting the two quantities FIRST (e.g. V=(4/3)πr³), before differentiating
Apply the chain rule systematically: dA/dt = (dA/dr) × (dr/dt), substituting known values only at the final step
Pay close attention to whether a rate is increasing (positive) or decreasing (negative) based on the problem's context
summary: Related rates problems are among the most practically important applications of differentiation, using the chain rule to connect real-world changing quantities like volume, area, and distance.
quick_revision: Set up an equation connecting the related quantities first
Differentiate using the chain rule: dA/dt = (dA/dr)(dr/dt)
Substitute known values only at the final step

explanation: Optimisation problems use differentiation to find the maximum or minimum value of a quantity subject to constraints, typically by expressing the quantity as a function of one variable and finding its stationary points.
key_concepts: Setting up the objective function from a constraint
Reducing to a single variable using the constraint
Finding and verifying the optimal value via calculus

definitions.definition: The process of finding the maximum or minimum value of a quantity using differentiation, typically subject to a given constraint.

formulas: Set dy/dx=0 to find critical values, verify using the second derivative or context

worked_examples.problem: A farmer has 100m of fencing for a rectangular field with one side against a wall. Maximise the area.
Find the dimensions of a cylinder with volume 500cm³ that minimises surface area, using S=2πr²+2πrh and V=πr²h.
worked_examples.answer: r = (1000/(4π))^(1/3) ≈ 4.30 cm (with h found by substituting back)

practice_questions.q: Two numbers sum to 30; maximise their product using calculus
practice_questions.answer: Let numbers be x, 30-x; P=x(30-x)=30x-x²; dP/dx=30-2x=0, x=15; max product=225

practice_questions.q: A rectangle has perimeter 40m; maximise its area using calculus
Minimise x²+1/x for x>0 using calculus
practice_questions.answer: Actually should be minimising a sum like x+1/x; d/dx(x+1/x)=1-1/x²=0, x=1; minimum value=2

practice_questions.q: State the general method for optimisation problems
practice_questions.answer: Set up the objective function, reduce to one variable using constraints, differentiate and set to zero, verify max/min

practice_questions.q: A box has square base x and height h, with volume 100. Express surface area S in terms of x alone.

exam_style_questions.q: An open-top box is to be made from a square sheet of cardboard with side 20cm, by cutting squares of side x from each corner and folding up the sides. Find the value of x that maximises the volume, and the maximum volume.
A cylindrical can must hold 330cm³. Find the radius that minimises the total surface area (including top and bottom), using V=πr²h and S=2πr²+2πrh.

common_mistakes: Errors setting up the initial constraint equation, leading to an incorrect objective function
Forgetting to reduce the objective function to a SINGLE variable before differentiating
Not verifying the found critical point is genuinely a maximum or minimum (skipping the second derivative check)
tips: Always express the quantity to be optimised as a function of just ONE variable, using the given constraint to eliminate the other(s)
Set the derivative to zero and solve, then ALWAYS verify the nature of the critical point using the second derivative or context
Real-world optimisation problems often have implicit domain restrictions (e.g. lengths must be positive) — check your solution makes physical sense
summary: Optimisation problems are the practical culmination of differentiation, combining constraint-based equation setup with stationary point analysis to solve real-world maximum/minimum problems.
quick_revision: Express the quantity as a function of ONE variable using the constraint
Differentiate, set to zero, solve
Verify max/min using the second derivative; check the solution makes physical sense

explanation: Maximum and minimum problems apply calculus-based optimisation techniques to a wide range of contexts, from geometry to economics, requiring careful translation of a word problem into a differentiable function.
key_concepts: Translating word problems into mathematical functions
Applying the full optimisation process systematically
Interpreting results correctly in the original problem's context

definitions.definition: A word problem requiring the use of calculus to find the maximum or minimum value of some quantity, subject to given conditions.

formulas: Full optimisation process: set up function, differentiate, solve, verify, interpret

worked_examples.problem: A company's profit is P(x)=-3x²+240x-2000, where x is units sold. Find the number of units maximising profit.
Find the maximum profit from the previous example

practice_questions.q: A cost function is C(x)=x²-20x+150. Find x minimising cost.
Find the minimum cost from the previous example
A revenue function is R(x)=100x-x². Find x maximising revenue.
Find the maximum revenue from the previous example
State the key first step in solving a maximum/minimum word problem
practice_questions.answer: Translate the problem into a mathematical function of a single variable

exam_style_questions.q: A rectangular enclosure is to be built using 200m of fencing, with the enclosure divided into two equal compartments by an additional fence parallel to one pair of sides. Find the dimensions maximising the total enclosed area.
exam_style_questions.answer: Let the enclosure have width x and length y, with the dividing fence also of length x; total fencing: 3x+2y=200, so y=(200-3x)/2; Area=xy=x(200-3x)/2=100x-1.5x²; dA/dx=100-3x=0, x=100/3; d²A/dx²=-3<0, confirming maximum; y=(200-100)/2=50; maximum area=(100/3)(50)=5000/3≈1666.7m²

exam_style_questions.q: A window is to be made in the shape of a rectangle topped by a semicircle, with total perimeter 10m. Find the radius of the semicircle that maximises the total area, given the perimeter constraint 2h+2r+πr=10 (h is the rectangle's height, r is the semicircle's radius, which equals half the rectangle's width).
exam_style_questions.answer: From the constraint: h=(10-2r-πr)/2=5-r-πr/2; Area=2rh+(1/2)πr²=2r[5-r-πr/2]+0.5πr²=10r-2r²-πr²+0.5πr²=10r-2r²-0.5πr²; dA/dr=10-4r-πr=0; r(4+π)=10; r=10/(4+π)≈1.40m

common_mistakes: Misreading or misinterpreting the word problem, leading to an incorrect initial equation setup
Errors in the algebraic manipulation required to reduce to a single-variable function
Forgetting to interpret the final numerical answer back in the context of the original problem, with correct units
tips: Read word problems carefully multiple times, identifying exactly what quantity is to be maximised/minimised and what the constraints are
Draw a diagram where helpful (especially for geometric optimisation problems) to correctly set up the relationships between variables
Always state your final answer clearly in the context of the original problem, including appropriate units
summary: Maximum and minimum problems are the practical, exam-relevant culmination of the entire Applications of Differentiation category, testing both calculus fluency and careful problem translation.
quick_revision: Carefully translate the word problem into a function
Apply the full optimisation process: differentiate, solve, verify
Interpret the final answer in context with correct units

explanation: Kinematics uses differentiation to relate displacement, velocity, and acceleration, since velocity is the derivative of displacement with respect to time, and acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
key_concepts: v = ds/dt (velocity is derivative of displacement)
a = dv/dt (acceleration is derivative of velocity)
Interpreting the sign of velocity and acceleration

definitions.definition: The study of motion using calculus, relating displacement s, velocity v=ds/dt, and acceleration a=dv/dt.

formulas: v = ds/dt
a = dv/dt = d²s/dt²

worked_examples.problem: Given s=t³-3t²+2t, find v and a as functions of t
Find the velocity at t=2 for s=t³-3t²+2t

practice_questions.q: Given s=t²-4t, find v(t)
Given s=t²-4t, find the time when v=0
Given v=3t²-2, find a(t)
Given s=5t-t², find a(t)
Given v=4-2t, find when the object is momentarily at rest

exam_style_questions.q: A particle moves such that its displacement is s=t³-6t²+9t (metres, t in seconds). Find the velocity and acceleration functions, and determine when the particle is momentarily at rest.
exam_style_questions.answer: v=3t²-12t+9; a=6t-12; at rest when v=0: 3t²-12t+9=0, t²-4t+3=0, (t-1)(t-3)=0; t=1 or t=3 seconds

exam_style_questions.q: For the particle in the previous question, find the acceleration at each time it is momentarily at rest, and interpret whether the particle is about to speed up or slow down at each instant.
exam_style_questions.answer: At t=1: a=6(1)-12=-6 (negative acceleration, so velocity is about to decrease, meaning the particle reverses into negative velocity — it was moving forward and is about to move backward); at t=3: a=6(3)-12=6 (positive acceleration, so velocity is about to increase from zero, meaning the particle starts moving forward again)

common_mistakes: Confusing displacement, velocity, and acceleration — always keep track of which quantity a given expression represents
Errors differentiating s(t) or v(t), especially with more complex polynomial or other function forms
Misinterpreting 'at rest' (v=0) as meaning the particle stays at rest, rather than being momentarily stationary before continuing to move
tips: Remember the chain of derivatives: s (displacement) → v (velocity, first derivative) → a (acceleration, second derivative)
'At rest' or 'momentarily stationary' means v=0 at that specific instant — the particle can (and often does) continue moving immediately afterward
Use the sign of a at the moment v=0 to determine whether the particle is about to move in the positive or negative direction next
summary: Kinematics is one of the most important real-world applications of differentiation, directly connecting the abstract concepts of rate of change to physical motion.
quick_revision: v = ds/dt
a = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
v=0: momentarily at rest (not necessarily permanently stopped)
related_topics: Rates of Change and Related Rates

explanation: Velocity is found by differentiating the displacement function with respect to time, giving the instantaneous rate at which position changes, with its sign indicating direction of motion.
key_concepts: v = ds/dt
Positive velocity: moving in positive direction; negative: moving in negative direction
Speed as the magnitude of velocity

definitions.definition: The rate of change of displacement with respect to time, v = ds/dt, a vector quantity including direction (sign).

formulas: v(t) = ds/dt

worked_examples.problem: Given s=4t²-3t, find v(t)
Find the velocity at t=1 for s=t³-5t

practice_questions.q: Given s=3t²+2t, find v(t)
Given s=t³-6t, find v(2)
Given s=5t-t², find v(3)
Given s=t², find when v=6
Given s=sin(t), find v(t)

exam_style_questions.q: A particle's displacement is given by s=2t³-9t²+12t. Find the velocity function, and determine the time interval(s) during which the particle is moving in the negative direction.
exam_style_questions.answer: v=6t²-18t+12=6(t²-3t+2)=6(t-1)(t-2); v<0 when (t-1)(t-2)<0, i.e. 1<t<2; the particle moves in the negative direction for 1<t<2 seconds

exam_style_questions.q: A ball's height is h=20t-5t², with velocity v=dh/dt. Find the velocity at t=0 and t=4, and interpret the sign of each in terms of the ball's motion.
exam_style_questions.answer: v=20-10t; at t=0: v=20 (positive, moving upward — this is the initial launch velocity); at t=4: v=20-40=-20 (negative, moving downward — the ball is falling back down)

common_mistakes: Confusing the sign of velocity with the sign of displacement (they represent different things)
Errors differentiating more complex displacement functions
Not correctly interpreting what a negative velocity means in the physical context (moving backward/downward, not 'negative speed')
tips: Velocity's sign indicates DIRECTION of motion, not whether the particle has moved a positive or negative total distance
Differentiate the displacement function carefully using standard differentiation rules for whatever function type is given
In context problems (like a ball thrown upward), interpret positive/negative velocity physically (e.g. upward vs downward)
summary: Velocity as the derivative of displacement is the foundational kinematics relationship, with its sign providing crucial directional information about motion.
quick_revision: v(t) = ds/dt
Positive v: moving in positive direction; negative v: moving in negative direction
Speed = |v| (magnitude only)

explanation: Acceleration is found by differentiating the velocity function with respect to time, giving the instantaneous rate of change of velocity, indicating whether the object is speeding up or slowing down.
key_concepts: a = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
Positive/negative acceleration relative to velocity's sign (speeding up vs slowing down)
Constant acceleration cases (as in standard SUVAT-type motion)

definitions.definition: The rate of change of velocity with respect to time, a = dv/dt, indicating how quickly velocity itself is changing.

formulas: a(t) = dv/dt = d²s/dt²

worked_examples.problem: Given v=6t-4, find a(t)
Given v=t²-3t, find a(2)

practice_questions.q: Given v=4t+1, find a(t)
Given v=t²-2t, find a(1)
Given v=3t²+2, find a(t)
Given v=5-3t, find a(t)
Given v=sin(t), find a(t)

exam_style_questions.q: A particle's velocity is v=3t²-12t+9. Find the acceleration function, and determine when the particle's acceleration is zero, interpreting this in terms of the velocity's behaviour at that instant.
exam_style_questions.answer: a=6t-12; a=0 when t=2; at this instant, the velocity is momentarily neither increasing nor decreasing (v itself is at a stationary point — specifically a minimum, since a changes from negative to positive here)

exam_style_questions.q: A car's velocity is modelled by v=20-2t for the first 10 seconds. Determine whether the car is speeding up or slowing down throughout this interval, using the relationship between the signs of v and a.
exam_style_questions.answer: a=dv/dt=-2 (constant, negative); since v=20-2t is positive for 0≤t<10 and a is negative, the velocity and acceleration have OPPOSITE signs, meaning the car is slowing down (decelerating) throughout this interval

common_mistakes: Confusing acceleration with velocity (different quantities, related by another derivative)
Errors interpreting whether an object is speeding up or slowing down (requires comparing the SIGNS of both velocity and acceleration, not just looking at acceleration alone)
Differentiation errors when v(t) is more complex
tips: An object speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the SAME sign, and slows down when they have OPPOSITE signs — always check both
Acceleration is the second derivative of displacement (or first derivative of velocity) — these are equivalent, just computed via different starting functions
Constant acceleration (as in standard SUVAT motion) corresponds to a linear velocity function
summary: Acceleration as the derivative of velocity completes the kinematics chain, with the relationship between the SIGNS of velocity and acceleration determining whether an object speeds up or slows down.
quick_revision: a(t) = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
Same sign (v,a): speeding up; opposite signs: slowing down
Constant a corresponds to a linear v(t)

explanation: Velocity-time and displacement-time graphs visually represent motion, with the gradient of a displacement-time graph giving velocity, and the gradient of a velocity-time graph giving acceleration — connecting graphical and calculus interpretations of motion.
key_concepts: Gradient of displacement-time graph = velocity
Gradient of velocity-time graph = acceleration
Area under a velocity-time graph = displacement

definitions.definition: A graph plotting displacement against time, whose gradient at any point gives the instantaneous velocity.

formulas: Gradient of s-t graph = v; Gradient of v-t graph = a; Area under v-t graph = displacement

worked_examples.problem: A displacement-time graph shows a straight line from (0,0) to (5,20). Find the constant velocity.
A velocity-time graph shows a straight line from (0,10) to (4,2). Find the constant acceleration.

practice_questions.q: A displacement-time graph is a horizontal line. What does this indicate about velocity?
practice_questions.answer: Velocity is zero (the object is stationary)

practice_questions.q: A velocity-time graph is a horizontal line above the x-axis. What does this indicate about acceleration?
On a v-t graph, what does the area under the curve between two times represent?
practice_questions.answer: The displacement during that time interval

practice_questions.q: A displacement-time graph curves upward increasingly steeply. What does this indicate about velocity?
On a v-t graph, a region below the x-axis represents what about displacement?
practice_questions.answer: Negative displacement (movement in the negative direction) during that interval

exam_style_questions.q: A velocity-time graph shows an object accelerating uniformly from rest to 20 m/s over 5 seconds, then travelling at constant velocity for 10 seconds, then decelerating uniformly to rest over 4 seconds. Sketch the key features of this graph and calculate the total displacement using areas.
exam_style_questions.answer: Phase 1 (acceleration): triangle, area=(1/2)(5)(20)=50m; Phase 2 (constant velocity): rectangle, area=20×10=200m; Phase 3 (deceleration): triangle, area=(1/2)(4)(20)=40m; total displacement=50+200+40=290m

exam_style_questions.q: A displacement-time graph for a particle shows the curve becoming less steep over time, eventually reaching a horizontal tangent, then becoming steeper again but sloping downward. Describe the particle's velocity and acceleration behaviour throughout, connecting this to the shape of the graph.
exam_style_questions.answer: Initially the particle has positive, decreasing velocity (graph less steep = velocity decreasing, but still positive = still moving forward), meaning negative acceleration (decelerating); at the horizontal tangent, velocity is momentarily zero (particle momentarily at rest); afterward, the downward slope indicates negative velocity (moving in the reverse direction), with increasing steepness indicating the magnitude of this negative velocity is increasing (accelerating in the negative direction)

common_mistakes: Confusing the gradient interpretation on an s-t graph (gives velocity) with that on a v-t graph (gives acceleration) — these are DIFFERENT graphs with different gradient meanings
Forgetting that area under a v-t graph gives DISPLACEMENT, not some other quantity
Misreading curved sections of a graph, especially confusing concavity with the sign of the gradient itself
tips: Always identify which type of graph you're looking at first (s-t or v-t) before interpreting gradient or area, since their meanings differ completely
Area under a v-t graph = displacement; area below the time-axis represents negative displacement (contributing negatively to net displacement)
A steepening curve on an s-t graph indicates increasing speed; a flattening curve indicates decreasing speed — connect this to the concept of the derivative (gradient) itself changing
summary: Motion graphs provide a visual, complementary perspective to the calculus-based kinematics equations, with gradient and area interpretations linking directly to velocity, acceleration, and displacement.
quick_revision: s-t graph gradient = velocity
v-t graph gradient = acceleration; area under v-t graph = displacement
Steepening/flattening curves indicate changing speed

images.description: A velocity-time graph showing three phases (acceleration, constant velocity, deceleration) as a trapezoid shape, with the area under each section shaded and labelled to represent displacement.
images.purpose: Demonstrates how the area under a velocity-time graph corresponds to displacement, and how gradient corresponds to acceleration in each phase.
